Open-book reference: DSP L01–L10 (full course)

Covers every lecture, L01 to L10, and replaces the weeks 1–4 strip of the earlier version. Notation follows the course: uppercase , for continuous time (CT); lowercase , for discrete time (DT). (rad/sample). The course defines sinc (MATLAB/numpy use , T9 Q1). = minimum passband gain, = maximum stopband gain (linear). “↑” marks . Sample Test 1 (50 min, 20 marks, open book) covered L02–L04; L05–L10 have never been tested.

L01 Overview: why DSP, and signal types

Advantage of digital (slide 6) Why (analogue vs digital filter case study, slides 7–8)
Flexibility (programmable) Analogue: a new cutoff needs a new and/or ; new filter type means a new circuit. Digital: just change
Accuracy, precision DSP computes with multiply-accumulate; no component tolerance
Low-cost implementation A long (high order) is cheap in software; high-order analogue filters are expensive
Reliability No drift or failure with time and temperature (analogue , drift)
Classification (slides 9–11) Meaning
Continuous-time / discrete-time , / , . DT usually from sampling; some are inherently DT (stock prices)
Continuous-valued / discrete-valued amplitude real / amplitude in a finite set (quantised)
Digital discrete-time and discrete-valued
Deterministic / random explicit formula (e.g. ) / described by a pdf (e.g. Gaussian, mean , variance )

P7. Linearity from observed input-output pairs (T2 Q2)

  1. Use time invariance to shift one known pair so its input lines up with another input.
  2. Test whether the inputs are scalar multiples or sums of each other.
  3. If linear, the outputs must be related the same way. One mismatch proves nonlinear. Matching pairs prove nothing in general.
